items.title: Vance tells Republicans to 'stop whining' about controversial Ohio attack ad
items.summary: The ad by Ohio Republican Vivek Ramaswamy features his Democratic rival's estranged mother, who she has not seen since her stepfather was charged with sexual abuse in her childhood.
items.content:
US Vice-President JD Vance has urged fellow Republicans to stop "whining" about a controversial attack ad that featured a Democratic candidate's estranged mother calling her a liar.

While campaigning in Ohio for Vivek Ramaswamy, the Republican candidate for governor, Vance said he was "a little bit disgusted" by criticism from members of his own party.

In the ad, Donna Arthur, the mother of Democratic candidate Amy Acton, said her daughter "lied her entire life". It does not mention that Arthur's husband was charged with raping Acton when she was a child.

The Ramaswamy campaign have claimed credit for the ad, and have paid millions to have it advertised around the state.

Acton's brother is among those who have condemned the ad, saying turning alleged sexual assault into "a political talking point" was a "despicable low".

Acton and her brother were removed from their mother's custody when her stepfather, Cledith Arthur, was arrested and charged in 1978.

That is when she last spoke to her mother, Acton said in an interview with The Vindicator, an Ohio news outlet. The Arthurs fled Ohio and Cledith Arthur was never prosecuted on the rape charge. He died in 2004.

When the ad featuring Donna Arthur was initially released to social media on Monday evening, it did not say who the video was paid for or authorised by. Ramaswamy confirmed on Tuesday that it came from his campaign, and he later pledged to spend $4m (£2.9m) to further air it.

Former South Carolina Governor Nikki Haley, who ran against Ramaswamy for the Republican nomination for president in 2024, said "he's a bad guy. It's a shame he continues to get away with it".

Vance, when asked by BBC News if he thought the ad was appropriate, answered: "It's not really my concern."

"What is my concern is who's going to govern the next generation of American government."

He also said he was "a little bit disgusted" by members of his own party who "are whining more about that advertisement than they are about what the congressional Democrats and other Democrats want to do to the United States of America".

Vance, a former Ohio senator, later defended the ad at a rally for Ramaswamy, saying: "Now the media and the Democrats in the state of Ohio are obsessed because guess what? Vivek Ramaswamy had the audacity to run a TV commercial which calls it out like it is, and calls Amy Acton a liar."

When asked about Ramaswamy's ad on Wednesday, Trump said: "I know nothing about it. I heard the mother went very rogue on the daughter."

He added: "It's a very unusual situation to have a mother hate a daughter that much. But I dont think that has anything to do with Vivek."

Acton's team released its own campaign ad on Tuesday, a video featuring her brother, Philip Stearns, recounting childhood abuse and saying "Amy always got the worst of it".

"Shame on Vivek," he says in the 30-second clip. "It's the contempt he has for Amy. It's the contempt he has for Ohio."

Other Republicans, including ones running for statewide office, have now criticised the ad.

Ohio Senator John Husted, who is up for re-election, told the Associated Press: "I would not have run that ad."

Ohio Secretary of Frank LaRose, who is running to be state auditor, was another Republican coming out against the ad.

"I will say that, you know, candidates will answer for their own ads, that, you know, I probably wouldn't run an ad like that, but every candidate gets to make their own decision," he told WSYX-TV , external in the city of Columbus.

Political attack ads are not a new feature of US politics, but David Lublin, a professor from American University's School of Public Affairs, told the BBC that "they have become more intense, and the boundaries have stretched in terms of what one attacks about".

Lublin said it was not new for relatives to be used against a political opponent, mentioning family members who testified against Robert F Kennedy Jr before he was confirmed as health secretary.

"But this is of a different order," he said. "They're estranged not over policy but over a rape allegation."

Lublin believes President Donald Trump's rhetoric and campaigns have helped act as a catalyst for the coarsening of American political discourse - mentioning the time Trump mocked a reporter in Ohio who had a disability.

"We live in an age where certainly many candidates can appear mean and even inappropriate at times," Lublin said, adding: "The key purpose of attack ads isn't necessarily to convert the followers of your opponent, but more to depress their turnout."

He expects the Ramaswamy attack ad to backfire, saying it could be an indication that his campaign is desperate to swing momentum in his favour in the increasingly competitive race for Ohio governor - even though a Democrat has not been elected governor there in over two decades.

Cook Political Report, a nonpartisan website that rates and tracks US elections, has moved the Ohio governor's race from "leans Republican" to "toss up", meaning neither candidate has a clear advantage.

items.title: Airbnb hosts can no longer make guests strip beds and wash dishes under new rules
items.summary: The updated policy will apply to all reservations booked on the accommodation site on or after 20 November.
items.content:
Airbnb has changed its rules to limit what property hosts may ask guests to do - including when it comes to cleaning.

The updated guidelines state that hosts can now set seven standard house rules and can also add other "reasonable" requests.

Airbnb states that guests - who are required to pay a cleaning fee - should not be asked to complete tasks normally done by a cleaner, including washing dishes and stripping beds.

The new rules will apply to all reservations booked on or after 20 November on the accommodation marketplace.

"House rules help guests understand what hosts expect, but we've heard from our community that they can be confusing, onerous and hard to manage," Airbnb told the BBC.

"So, we've redesigned them to make them easier to discover and clearer to set, alongside a new policy that keeps requests reasonable, with no surprises."

According to the new requirements on the Airbnb website, hosts are generally not allowed to ask guests to complete tasks that "require significant effort or time, or would typically be performed by a cleaner, including stripping the bed, taking trash offsite, or washing and putting away dishes".

The company said it may grant exceptions in some circumstances. For example, guests can be asked to limit shower time if there are local drought-related water restrictions.

A property's rules will be displayed to guests more prominently moving forward and will appear in the guests' reservation reminders.

Contracts will only be allowed in limited circumstances, including when required by law or homeowners association rules.

While a host will not be able to impose fines, they remain in control of their house rules and requests, the company said.

If a host's request does not follow Airbnb policies, the issue will be flagged and the owner can appeal if they disagree.

Guests have for years complained about unreasonable tasks they we required to complete before departure, especially as they are required to pay cleaning fees.

TikTok videos from Airbnb hosts Cassie and Jon that show them closely inspecting their rental property in the US state of Georgia after guests leave have gone viral recently for their attention to detail.

One video from the couple, for example, accuses guests of "disrespecting the house rules" for leaving a television remote out of place.

They have been criticised for their strict rules and high standards but said in response that their content had been misinterpreted

Their videos have inspired other content creators to parody stringent hosts.

Airbnb fined £56m by Spain for advertising unlicensed properties

items.title: Postgres recovery_prefetch can cause outages
items.summary: Article URL: https://ardentperf.com/2026/10/20/postgres-recovery_prefetch-considered-harmful-and-causing-outages/ Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50188614 Points: 13 # Comments: 0
items.content:
Another story of something I saw in the field which surprised me. Turns out recovery_prefetch can cause outages.

Something which has been happening quietly in the background all the time, but we didn’t notice until we looked close enough to see it.

After a lot of work I discovered this was partly a case where someone had dropped an email to the postgres hackers list years ago “hey what about this” and everyone thought “nah it can’t be that bad” … and now here we are seeing production outages!

Exhibit A: Feb 2021, while the feature was being developed, a year and a half before it shipped, Stephen Frost

https://www.postgresql.org/message-id/20210214231815.GO27507@tamriel.snowman.net

Exhibit B: Mar 2025, clear report from the field, Michael Zhilin (Postgres Pro)

https://www.postgresql.org/message-id/9bdb428a-fc8e-4801-8fff-1ad0bc6fa76b%40postgrespro.ru

Both of these emails were on the right track, but didn’t quite get the complete picture yet.

First: FPI/FPW is ubiquitous today. While it’s very expensive in terms of performance, it’s the only way Postgres has of protecting from torn writes on OS restarts. As a result, the majority of production Postgres installations today (community oss version) enable this.

Second: synchronous replication is becoming more common. There are really only two ways to completely protect community open source postgres against data loss on hardware failures: (1) storage layer replication with oss tech like DRBD or expensive proprietary storage & clustering technology or (2) database layer protection with postgres synchronous replication. The second option is the normal solution with kubernetes and commodity hardware.

Third: something that hasn’t previously been diagnosed/reported – the problem with recovery_prefetch isn’t just about FPIs, it’s also about the fact that when the primary instance does large sequential I/O, recovery_prefetch converts those operations into 8k random reads. For the same number of bytes read, this amplifies IOPS as much as 16x on replicas. This can easily exhaust available IOPS, causing replicas to significantly lag after write activity.

The read IOPS amplification combined with Postgres design for synchronous replication is what turns recovery_prefetch into an actual outage-inducing killer. And it turns out this is trivial to reproduce once you know the steps.

It really is this easy to consistently reproduce this outage. https://github.com/ardentperf-labs/walreceiver-outage-repro

And for what it’s worth, VACUUM itself is quite capable of producing write activity too. The recipe for an outage is simply “enough bad luck”: a network glitch that interrupts streaming replication at the same time as a burst of write activity.

To understand why the whole system hangs, it really comes down to two simple things: (1) synchronous replication and (2) the core “state machine” that defines a Postgres Standby Server.

Remember that with synchronous replication, we’re depending on at least one healthy standby server – otherwise we can’t take writes. (We want to guarantee durability to clients and ensure every transaction is on a remote machine before commit.)

The core standby server state machine is defined in src/backend/access/transam/xlogrecovery.c :

Basically, when a Postgres standby switches into WAL-restore mode, it will not go back to streaming until it’s caught up.

A burst of write activity combined with IOPS amplification on all the replicas that causes significant lag can easily mean the database won’t start streaming again for hours .

The IOPS amplification is very clear. Here are the disk stats for the primary (maybe 5 minutes around 300 IOPS):

Here are the disk status for the replica/standby during the same time period (40 minutes at the disk limit of 500 IOPS):

These charts don’t illustrate it, but the number of bytes read from disk is about the same.

What happens if we disable recovery_prefetch ? (Note that FPWs remain enabled.)

https://github.com/ardentperf-labs/walreceiver-outage-repro/blob/main/variations/README.md#recovery_prefetchoff

There’s still the pause during UPDATE but we didn’t see the long pause after UPDATE completes.

There is no burst of read IOPS, and the standby server basically stays caught up – applying the 5% update in less than 10 minutes.

Right now, I’m leaning toward disabling the recovery_prefetch setting across the board but I want to see where the discussions go. I think its benefits are a little dubious with FPWs enabled by default.

Here’s a more detailed refresher on the various processes involved in the core restore and replay logic of a postgres standby server.

Importantly, note the direction of the arrow between the WAL sender and WAL receiver. With synchronous replication in Postgres this connection is critical – the primary can’t accept writes without it. It’s also very fragile, because if the connection disappears the primary can only sit and wait, blocking all writes, hoping a standby will reconnect soon!

This is a reason to consider two standbys and quorum commit (ANY 1) with postgres. While it does increase cost to run with three total replicas instead of two, it significantly increases the robustness of the database.

This reminds me of a related issue I hit with a customer on PostgreSQL 18.x. It’s a different trigger than recovery_prefetch, but it seems to involve the same logic around WaitForWALToBecomeAvailable and the standby state machine.

Setup: a hot standby created with pg_basebackup using a physical replication slot, with recovery_min_apply_delay = ‘7d’ added later, so we could recover from user errors (e.g., an accidental Friday Night delete noticed on Monday). After the first replica restart, streaming worked as expected: WAL arrived in real time and was replayed 7 days later, as intended.

After an OS update and reboot, the standby came up fine but never started the walreceiver. Since the delayed replay meant everything it needed was already in local pg_wal, it apparently never saw a reason to fetch more. Meanwhile pg_wal on the primary kept growing, held back by the slot, and nothing was streamed.

I found no way to force the walreceiver to start in this setup, other than waiting for the delayed replay to consume all the replica pg_wal (up to 7 days).

So, with replication, some settings can bite you at an unexpected moment…

items.title: New Mexico sues Epstein lawyer and accountant, accusing them of hiding his sex crimes
items.summary: Both men have denied having any knowledge of Epstein's crimes and their attorney rejected the lawsuit as "categorically false".
items.content:
Prosecutors in the US state of New Mexico have filed a civil lawsuit against two longtime aides of Jeffrey Epstein, accusing the men of profiting from the late financier's sex trafficking ring.

Lawyer Darren Indyke and accountant Richard Kahn are the sole executors of Epstein's estate, controlling all his wealth and possessions. They have denied any role in his crimes.

New Mexico Attorney General Raúl Torrez says they played a key role in concealing abuse at Epstein's remote Zorro Ranch near the city of Santa Fe, and that they continue to earn money while victims seek accountability.

The lawsuit is separate to the state's ongoing criminal probe into Epstein, which was re-launched in February.

An attorney representing both Indyke and Kahn told the BBC that they "emphatically reject" the claims in the lawsuit.

The lawsuit was filed in New Mexico on Wednesday under the federal Trafficking Victims Protection Act and New Mexico Racketeering Act.

During a news conference, Torrez argued that the two men are blocking efforts by Epstein's victims to seek compensation from his fortune, estimated at roughly $635m (£474m) at the time of his death.

"Those resources rightfully belong in the hands of survivors - there should be no distribution of Mr Epstein's remaining assets to people like Mr Indyke and Mr Kahn for participation in what I think is one of the most horrific criminal enterprises in modern America," he said.

Both men worked with Epstein for decades, and have previously testified to Congress that they were unaware of the crimes he committed alongside accomplice Ghislane Maxwell.

Their attorney Daniel Weiner said in a statement to the BBC that, "they are confident that they will prevail on the claims asserted against them".

"Both Mr Indyke and Mr Kahn reject as categorically false the allegations that they knowingly facilitated or assisted Mr Epstein in his sexual abuse or trafficking of women, or that they were aware of Mr Epstein's actions while they provided legal or accounting services to him," Weiner said.

He added that the New Mexico prosecutor never asked to speak to either man "before filing this baseless lawsuit", and that they both have "cooperated with any and all investigations when asked to do so".

Jeffrey Epstein had two key aides - why do they still control his money and secrets?

Epstein tried to buy a palace in Morocco days before his arrest in 2019

The two aides were named as co-executors in August 2019 by Epstein, just two days before he killed himself in jail while awaiting trial on child sex-trafficking charges.

He revised his will to transfer all his wealth into a trust named after the year of his birth, which the lawyer and accountant would administer.

In their role as executors, Indyke and Kahn agreed to fund compensation packages for survivors that included conditions that prevented survivors who accepted funds from taking further legal action against them personally. Other claims are still outstanding.

As beneficiaries of the trust, the men could also be paid tens of millions of dollars each from whatever remains when the claims are settled.

In his remarks, Torrez alleged that Epstein's crimes were "made possible by handlers, by lawyers, by accountants, by others who have yet to face real consequence".

"Jeffrey Epstein did not operate alone, and his death does not end the pursuit of accountability for the people who helped make his crimes possible," he said.

"Those who allegedly enabled this exploitation should not be allowed to profit from it while survivors continue to live with its consequences," he added.

items.title: Guerra in Iran, le news di oggi. Attacco su aeroporto in Arabia Saudita. Tre navi a fuoco a Hormuz
items.summary: Arabia Saudita: ambasciata Usa ordina di lasciare Paese
items.content:
Tre imbarcazioni hanno preso fuoco nella notte a ovest dello Stretto di Hormuz dopo aver urtato mine navali. Due palestinesi sono stati uccisi e molti altri feriti, uno dei quali in modo grave, quando un drone israeliano ha lanciato un missile vicino al quartier generale dell'Unrwa, a ovest di Gaza City.

Attacco su aeroporto in Arabia Saudita, un morto e otto feriti

Le Guardie Rivoluzionarie iraniane hanno reso noto di aver attaccato quattro navi che "hanno commesso violazioni, utilizzato una rotta illegale nello Stretto di Hormuz e trasferito petrolio da una nave all'altra nel Golfo Persico". Secondo l'Iran, le navi sono ora avvolte dalle fiamme. I pasdaran hanno anche minacciato gli Stati Uniti: "L'esercito americano deve capire che se questa tendenza continua, la portata del conflitto si espanderà e raggiungerà le basi degli stessi aggressori nella regione".

Tre imbarcazioni hanno preso fuoco nella notte a ovest dello Stretto di Hormuz dopo aver urtato mine navali. Lo ha riferito la marina dei Pasdaran iraniani, secondo quanto riferito dall'agenzia russa Tass.

"No, non credo che stiamo negoziando con l'Iran. In un modo o nell'altro, qualcosa accadrà molto presto. La maggior parte delle persone pensa che succederà dopo le elezioni (di midterm, ndr) e vedremo cosa accadrà". Lo ha detto il presidente Usa, Donald Trump, rispondendo alle domande dei giornalisti.

Media: Usa e Israele pensano a nuovi attacchi in Iran dopo le midterm

IGli eserciti di Stati Uniti e Israele hanno elaborato piani specifici per nuovi attacchi all'Iran dopo le elezioni di americane di midterm. Lo ha rivelato il New York Times, citando funzionari statunitensi e fonti, dopo che lunedì scorso decine di caccia israeliani hanno sorvolato la Siria e l'Iraq, raggiungendo il confine con l'Iran. Il Segretario alla Difesa Usa, Pete Hegseth, ha incontrato il primo ministro Benjamin Netanyahu in Israele questa settimana per discutere di nuovi attacchi, secondo quanto riferito dai funzionari statunitensi. Tra gli obiettivi ci sarebbero le infrastrutture energetiche iraniane, gli impianti nucleari e l'arsenale di missili e droni. Alcuni funzionari affermano che un'altra serie di attacchi su larga scala potrebbe spingere l'economia iraniana sull'orlo del collasso e costringere Teheran a concessioni diplomatiche dopo quasi otto mesi di conflitto.

Attacco su aeroporto in Arabia Saudita, un morto e otto feriti

Un morto e otto feriti è il bilancio di un attacco sull'aeroporto internazionale 'Re Fahd' di Dammam, nella parte orientale dell'Arabia Saudita. Lo ha annunciato l'Autorità generale per l'aviazione civile del Paese. L'attacco ha provocato la morte di un residente, mentre altre otto persone sono rimaste ferite e sono state trasportate in ospedale. In un comunicato, l'autorità ha riferito che le ferite riportate vanno da "lievi a gravi" e che sono in corso le valutazioni sui danni materiali subiti dallo scalo. Non è stato specificato di che tipo di attacco si sia trattato; tuttavia, negli ultimi giorni, gli aeroporti del Regno sono stati più volte presi di mira da proiettili lanciati dagli Houthi yemeniti, sostenuti dall'Iran.

I combattimenti in Yemen hanno costretto quasi 260 mila persone a lasciare le proprie case dall'inizio di agosto. Lo ha riferito il portavoce della segreteria generale dell'Onu, Stephane Dujarric. Quasi la metà degli sfollati ha cercato rifugio nel governatorato di Taiz.

Secondo il Ministero della Salute dell'enclave, negli ultimi 24 ore gli attacchi israeliani hanno ucciso sette palestinesi a Gaza e ne hanno feriti altri 24. Da quando è entrato in vigore il "cessate il fuoco" a Gaza nell'ottobre 2025, gli attacchi israeliani hanno ucciso 1.534 palestinesi e ne hanno feriti 5.486, ha affermato il ministero. Nello stesso periodo, le squadre di soccorso hanno recuperato dalle macerie anche 841 corpi. Il ministero ha stimato il bilancio complessivo della guerra israeliana contro Gaza dall'ottobre 2023 a 74.494 morti e 175.604 feriti.

Mo. Cisgiordania, arrestati ed espulsi padre e figlio italiani

Due cittadini italiani, Manuel Tartarotti e suo padre Alberto, di 35 anni e 67 anni, sono stati detenuti per oltre un giorno dalla polizia israeliana in Cisgiordania con l'accusa di terrorismo e in seguito espulsi. A darne notizia un portale di informazione altoatesino. Il fermo dei due, originari di bolzano, sarebbe avvenuto nella zona di Massafer Yatta. Secondo Salto.Bz, padre e figlio si trovavano in Cisgiordania da domenica per consegnare fondi raccolti in italia a Youth of Sumud, associazione di volontariato che nel 2024 ha vinto il premio langer.La polizia israeliana ci ha chiesto i documenti, poi hanno preso me e mio padre, ci hanno bendati e ci hanno caricati su un furgone militare", ha raccontato manuel al portale altoatesino. "Non ci hanno detto dove ci portavano, io sono stato preso e picchiato nel retro del mezzo"

Due palestinesi sono stati uccisi e molti altri feriti, uno dei quali in modo grave, in serata quando un drone israeliano ha lanciato un missile vicino al quartier generale dell'Unrwa nel quartiere meridionale di al-Rimal, a ovest di Gaza City. Lo scrive Wafa. L'attacco ha preso di mira un palestinese in sella a una bicicletta elettrica e un gruppo di passanti. L'ospedale Al-Shifa, nella parte occidentale di Gaza City, ha riferito di aver ricevuto i corpi dei due morti insieme ai feriti, tra cui una persona in condizioni critiche.

items.title: Japan is known for world-class events - but the Asian Games were chaotic
items.summary: Hotel chaos, transport mishaps and diplomatic blunders cast a spotlight on organisers and the firm hired to deliver the games.
items.content:
From the Olympics to Tokyo's annual video game convention, Japan has a strong track record of hosting major international events. But this year's Asian Games in Nagoya and the wider Aichi Prefecture were marred by problems.

There were diplomatic blunders, transport errors and accommodation chaos. In comment fields online, some branded it the "worst Games in history" and urged a "full investigation".

Prof Kozo Tomiyama, who studies major sporting events at Osaka University, believes organisers were unable to handle the unexpected.

"If these problems damage international confidence in Japan's ability to operate sporting events, they could also affect Japan's ability to attract international competitions in the future," he warned.

The deputy director general of the Games, Takaaki Omi, admitted organisers had faced a range of unforeseen issues, but insisted they took on feedback and made improvements.

Before the tournament had even begun, participants were complaining about too few rooms and poor-quality accommodation.

Organisers had decided to forgo building a traditional athletes' village to cut costs, and were instead housing participants in hotels and container-style units across Nagoya. A top Korean basketball official said tall athletes housed in the containers were struggling to "stretch their legs out on the beds" .

Last-minute additions to the total number of participants strained the city's capacity so much that an Italian cruise ship with 1,500 cabins was used to fill the gap.

The organising committee had initially arranged accommodation for up to 15,000 delegation members "in accordance with the host city contract", Omi told the BBC. But as other sports were added, the number grew by 2,000 to a total of 17,000 .

Organisers initially claimed there was "simply nowhere" to put up the late influx and told them to make their own arrangements - before backpedalling and releasing a joint statement with the Olympic Council of Asia promising that all "17,000-plus" guests would get "Games-appropriate accommodation".

Over the course of the Games, athletes were bussed to the wrong venues and the North Korean anthem was played for the South Korean men's hockey team . During the men's football gold medal ceremony, the South Korean flag was not raised properly. Taiwan's sports minister found himself temporarily barred from a flag-raising event.

In the last days of the Games, volunteers received an email inviting them to the closing ceremony free of charge. But later an organiser said the decision to distribute free tickets was still under review and had not been approved.

Omi admitted the string of incidents at the event - which was bigger than the Paris Olympics by number of participants - had caused significant inconvenience for some delegations.

"Hosting and managing an event of this scale was a major challenge for us, and each day involved addressing a range of unexpected issues and challenges," he said.

"During the Games, we also listened carefully to feedback from the athletes who were actually using the facilities and responded promptly with necessary improvements and measures."

As soon as these issues began to surface, local media pointed fingers at the company managing venue operations: the Japanese subsidiary of France's GL Events.

GL Events had won the 63bn yen (£306m; $405m) contract over Dentsu Group, an advertising giant with a long history of successfully running sporting events in Japan that had been sidelined after a criminal bid-rigging conviction.

A source told Kyodo news agency that GL Events was "overwhelmingly cheaper" than alternative providers.

Last week the Tokyo Shimbun newspaper accused the firm of aggressively cutting corners on hiring, resulting in a shortage of experienced staff capable of managing the issues which arose. The personnel that were recruited were not properly trained, the newspaper alleged.

But organiser Takaaki Omi stressed that GL Events "has experience in international sporting events, including the Paris Olympic Games".

"We believe the necessary competition environment was in place by the start of competition, including thorough discussions and co-ordination with GL Events," he told the BBC.

Prof Tomiyama said he didn't think it was right to "simply conclude that GL events did not have sufficient experience with international competitions". He believes the issue stemmed from the "extremely broad" scope of responsibility they were given.

"Also, because this was a negotiated contract rather than a competitive tender, it's important to examine the criteria organisers used to assess the contractor's capabilities, as well as how they supervised the contractor after the contract was awarded," Tomiyama added.

GL Events did not respond to repeated BBC requests for comment.

Watching organisers play whack-a-mole as they rushed to address each new concern which popped up throughout the Games felt deeply out of line with what the world has come to expect from a major Japanese event.

It's far from the "omotenashi" spirit - Japan's whole-hearted hospitality that is almost an art form - they might have wanted to showcase.

Officials ended up having to send a formal apology to South Korea for the series of mishaps affecting that particular delegation.

But Olympic Council of Asia director general Husain al-Musallam was keen to highlight the 54 new world records achieved at the Games - in swimming, weightlifting, and shooting - as proof they were a hit.

"This achievement does not come without the best environment that the organising committee created for the athletes," he said. "The athletes cannot perform if they don't sleep good, the athletes cannot perform if they don't have good transportation."

Glitches have continued at the ongoing Para Games, where the wrong national anthems were played at three events. Nagoya Mayor Ichiro Hirosawa, who is also deputy head of the Games organising committee, called it "unacceptable" and offered his apologies.

Prof Tomiyama hopes organisers will take lessons from the past few weeks to deliver higher-quality sporting events in the future.

items.title: Security Disclosure
items.summary: Article URL: https://blog.railway.com/p/security-disclosure-wednesday-october-21st Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50188228 Points: 396 # Comments: 231
items.content:
Earlier this morning, Railway detected anomalous activity involving systems that store customer environment variables. After further investigation, our investigation to date indicates that an unauthorized third party may have accessed encrypted environment variables and, for some of them, obtained the decrypted contents. Environment variables may contain secrets such as API keys or database and registry credentials.

We believe this is part of a series of attacks recently targeting platform companies with the aim of compromising AI inference providers. We have notified these upstream providers to revoke all keys proactively, as we take these kinds of events extremely seriously.

While our initial analysis suggests the impact may be limited to a subset of users, we are nevertheless recommending that all users take the actions described below as a precaution to protect your systems while we complete our review.

What you should do: As such, we strongly recommend that you immediately roll all environment variables, including any API keys, stored in Railway, as well as any private registry credentials, and review logs for those services for unusual activity.

All deployments are paused while we investigate. Until builds are restored, you will not be able to roll out new versions. We apologize for this inconvenience. Follow this incident to be notified when builds resume.

As we confirm which accounts were affected, we will contact those customers directly by email with additional details.

We will provide new updates on this announcement, and on status.railway.com as we narrow the scope of impact.

items.title: Meta fined $25bn for 'lies' over user data privacy
items.summary: The fine is the largest to date against Facebook's owner, larger than an $18bn deal with California.
items.content:
Meta, the company behind Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp has been hit with its largest fine ever for its business practices.

A judge in New Mexico on Wednesday ordered the company to pay $25bn (£18.6bn) following a two-week trial earlier this year that found it had spent years lying to the public about how it handled Facebook user data.

"The lies extend beyond Facebook's data practices as well," the judge said, adding they went to "the heart of Facebook's core business practices".

Meta's head lawyer CJ Mahoney said the ruling made it "all but impossible to do business in the state of New Mexico". The company intends to appeal, a move Mahoney said will be successful.

The fine is the largest to date against Meta, which has either been fined or agreed to settle several other lawsuits this year, including an $18bn deal with California over child safety.

New Mexico's lawsuit stemmed from the role of Meta, then still doing business as Facebook, in what became known as the Cambridge Analytica scandal.

That firm utilised data and information from millions of Facebook users as part of its work in political consulting, including on work related to the 2016 US Presidential election, which saw Donald Trump elected for the first time.

New Mexico had also accused Meta of intentionally misleading the public on how it benefitted from content that included hate speech, and how such rules against it were enforced. The jury found the company had intentionally misled the public on those claims, too.

Meta disputed those accusations. "At its core, this lawsuit seeks to impose a tax on speech to enforce new rules for what people can say online," Mahoney added.

Lawyers for New Mexico sued the company over many statements Meta executives had made over the years that user data was never shared with or accessed by third parties without a user's permission, when in reality it had been.

They claimed that the entire population of the state, roughly two million people, was impacted by Meta's dishonesty regarding the way it controlled user data. A jury found that Meta had violated state laws more than 40 million times.

"For too long, powerful technology companies have operated as though their size and influence put them beyond the reach of the law," New Mexico Attorney General Raúl Torrez said on Wednesday.

"Today's result makes clear that no corporation is too powerful to be held accountable."

The state lawyers sought up to $40bn in fines against Meta. Meta had argued anything beyond $3.4bn would be unconstitutional.

Judge Francis Mathew on Wednesday was direct in his decision to fine Meta an amount roughly equal to its profits each quarter.

He said Meta's violations of law and misrepresentations to the public about how their Facebook data was used and shared were "willful" and spanned "more than 11 years", stretching from 2010 to 2021.

Communications between senior executives, including Mark Zuckerberg, were "designed to mislead the public", Judge Mathew wrote in his order.

While the full amount of the penalty against Meta, based on thousands of violations of state law, was calculated as $219bn, Judge Mathew reduced the penalty to the $25bn fine.

It follows a $5bn fine levied by the US Federal Trade Commission in 2019 against the company over its data privacy practices.

Campaigners welcome Meta and YouTube's defeat in landmark social media addiction trial

Meta fined $567m in largest child safety ruling against social media giant

New Mexico has been one of Meta's most notable adversaries in court. The state this year also fined Meta almost $1bn for misleading the public about the safety of its social media platforms for children.

The judge overseeing that lawsuit ultimately compared Meta to an industrial polluter of the air, with its form of pollution being "the psychological harm and sexual exploitation of children".

As large as the fines against Meta are, the company is spending much more on infrastructure as it works to catch up with other tech companies in the artificial intelligence (AI) race.

Zuckerberg said during a call with financial analysts that Meta's consumer-focused AI tool Muse was already being used by 10 million people.

"Growing Muse to serve billions of people is both our mission and our strategy," Zuckerberg said.

To that end, Meta expects to spend at least $135bn this year on mostly AI projects, but could spend up to $145bn.

The company is spending so much on AI that it reported negative cash flow of more than $2bn - an apparent first for Meta since it listed on the public stock market 14 years ago, according to a BBC review of its past financial documents.

Cash flow represents the money a company retains after paying for operations and investments. So, Meta is now spending more than it brings in, even as it brings in more money than ever.

Meta's revenue increased 26% for July to September compared to a year ago, hitting $64.5bn. Its profits also tripled to $9.8bn.

Still, the company intends to spend more on AI investments. Meta's chief financial officer Susan Li announced a new stock split on the call, in which existing Meta shareholders will receive one new share on non-voting stock.

Li said the new class of stock was not yet intended for one specific investment, but she alluded to ongoing costs related to AI and said the company could use "more funding flexibility" next year.

items.title: La studentessa Erasmus violentata a Milano, c'è un fermo
items.summary: La 21enne tedesca aggredita all'alba di giovedì scorso in zona parco Trotter
items.content:
C'è un fermo per lo stupro a Milano di una studentessa tedesca in Erasmus violentata in zona Parco Trotter. Si tratta di un cittadino peruviano di 31 anni, irregolare e senza fissa dimora, fermato martedì con l'accusa di avere abusato della 21enne poco prima dell'alba di giovedì scorso in via Giacosa. La notizia, anticipata online da Corriere della Sera, la Repubblica e il Giorno, è stata confermata all'ANSA da fonti vicine all'inchiesta.

A portare i carabinieri sulle tracce del 31enne è statto il ritrovamento di uno zainetto nella zona dell'aggresione. All'interno, gli investigatori — coordinati dai pm Maria Letizia Mannella e Alfonso Serritiello — hanno recuperato lo scontrino di un supermercato. L'analisi delle telecamere del negozio ha consentito agli inquirenti di isolare il volto dell'aggressore, poi identificato grazie alla tesserina sim di un telefono trovata all'interno dello stesso zaino. Setacciati anche i filmati dei sistemi di videosorveglianza, l'uomo è stato interrogato oggi nell'udienza di convalida dal gip Fabrizio Filice che depositerà domani la decisione.

items.title: Missiles hit Kyiv after Russia agrees to US call to resume Ukraine peace talks
items.summary: Moscow says it is "ready in principle" to resume peace talks and US President Donald Trump says the world is "the closest we've been" to ending the war.
items.content:
Ukraine's capital has come under a new missile attack, hours after Russia said it was "ready in principle" to resume peace talks and the US president said the world was "the closest we've been" to ending the war.

Several houses were hit on Wednesday night, injuring six people, Kyiv Mayor Vitaliy Klitschko said.

The attack came amid a new diplomatic push led by Donald Trump's envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner. Witkoff met Russia's President Vladimir Putin in the city of St Petersburg on Wednesday - a day after meeting Ukraine's leader.

Three-way talks were paused in February, after which Russia stepped up attacks as Ukraine ran out of Western-supplied interceptors to defend against missiles.

Speaking on Wednesday, Trump said: "The other day I was talking to Vladimir Putin about settling his war with Ukraine, which I think we're getting closer to, by the way, maybe now the closest we've been."

The US president has so far failed to bring the Russia-Ukraine war to an end despite his repeated comments that he would be able to achieve this.

Rosenberg: US diplomatic push offers little hope for imminent Ukraine peace

Trump's special envoy Witkoff went to St Petersburg after meeting Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky as well as the leaders of Norway and Finland in the Norwegian capital, Oslo, on Tuesday.

It is not clear what specific proposals Witkoff brought to Putin, but Zelensky said after the talks that "strong" security guarantees for Ukraine and energy ceasefire proposals had been discussed.

Putin's aide Yuri Ushakov said their ideas were not very "useful".

Top officials from Russia, Ukraine and the US have held several rounds of talks aimed at ending the war.

Russia blamed last month's "massive" Ukrainian strikes during its general elections for their disruption.

Putin launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, and Moscow currently controls about 20% of Ukrainian territory.

Speaking to reporters after Wednesday's talks in St Petersburg, Ushakov suggested that a new round could be held around 10 November in Abu Dhabi, the capital of the United Arab Emirates.

He stressed that the talks must focus on "building a security system for Russia and Ukraine after the end of the conflict."

Ushakov also told reporters that Putin reiterated to Witkoff that Russian troops were advancing everywhere across the vast front line and had a "strategic initiative".

Ukraine and its European allies have disputed Putin's claim, pointing to a virtual stalemate on the front.

On Wednesday, Zelensky said he would accept a deal that would freeze the war along the current front line.

"We call it 'ceasefire' or 'stop killings' like President Trump called it. Freeze and stop. And of course this is minimum what we need from Russia today," he told Fox News, adding that security guarantees for Ukraine could be discussed after this.

Witkoff described the latest talks as "constructive", while Kushner, who was participating via a video link, said: "There is still hard work ahead, but we have a real opportunity to move beyond this war and build a framework for lasting peace, security, and prosperity for generations to come."

The talks were held amid a growing row between Ukraine and the US.

Trump has said it is time for Ukraine to get a new president, and most recently "for somebody else to negotiate on behalf of Ukraine".

He has blamed Ukraine's attacks on Russian oil refineries for fuel prices which have been rising since the start of the US-led war on Iran.

He was also heavily criticised by Democratic and some Republican lawmakers after lifting sanctions on Russia - allowing it to release tonnes of diesel "to the American and global marketplace".

That was despite signing legislation to authorise fresh US sanctions and tariffs on nations that import Russian oil and gas just weeks earlier.

Zelensky - and Ukraine's European allies - criticised Trump's move.

Last week, Kyiv accused Washington of withholding critical intelligence to warn Ukrainians about incoming Russian ballistic missile launches, resulting in many civilian deaths.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio on Tuesday rejected such accusations as "scandalous", and Zelensky said after the Oslo talks that intelligence sharing "works now" .

Ukraine's military has also complained of speed restrictions to the US satellite internet network Starlink, which constricted its ability to use drones to conduct strikes against Russia.

US officials have denied having requested such a slowdown and a bipartisan group of US senators has called for an urgent investigation .

Before the Putin-Witkoff talks started, Russia released Stephen Hubbard, a 74-year-old American citizen who had been given a jail sentence of nearly seven years for allegedly fighting on behalf of Ukraine.

Trump said the former teacher was "on his way back home" and "there was no 'swap' necessary", while Witkoff called Putin a "humanitarian" for agreeing the release.

When asked by a BBC reporter whether he agreed with such a description of the Kremlin leader, US Vice-President JD Vance said: "I agree with Steve Witkoff saying something nice to a person who just released an American hostage.

"Whether you agree with the underlying sentiment or not, Steve Witkoff is a diplomat. His job is to go over there and get a job done. I care much less about what Steve said than about the fact that he is bringing an American hostage home to his family."

US citizen Stephen Hubbard freed by Russia as Trump envoy meets Putin

items.title: Champions League: l'Inter in 10 torna a vincere, primi punti con lo Shakhtar
items.summary: Rosso a Bastoni per doppia ammonizione, ci pensa Carlos Augusto
items.content:
L'Inter torna a vincere in Champions League e lo fa con una partita che per come è evoluta può essere davvero quella della svolta. I nerazzurri si impongono contro lo Shakthar giocando in inferiorità numerica per 20' per l'espulsione di Bastoni, mostrando tenacia, caparbietà, voglia di riscatto. Caratteristiche che in altre occasioni sono venute meno. Segna Carlos Augusto, certificando un avvio di stagione d'oro, assist di Mkhitaryan anche lui in splendida forma. Prossimo avversario il Feyenoord, ma l'Inter ha allontanato fantasmi e statistiche negative, ha cancellato lo 'zero' nella casella punti e ora può riprendere la sua corsa.

Certo, non è stata una partita perfetta, nel primo tempo è mancato un po' di brio ma la ripresa fa ben sperare e contava solo la vittoria. Pronti, via e l'Inter sfiora subito il vantaggio con Thuram ma il portiere dello Shakhtar dimostra di essere entrato immediatamente in partita e devia in angolo. Poi è Calhanoglu a mettersi in mostra ma senza inquadrare la porta. Al 21' altra nitida occasione da gol con un rasoterra di Bonny che viene però parato. L'approccio è prorompente. Poi però con il passare dei minuti esce anche lo Shakhtar in particolare con Pedrinho. Ma il numero dieci della squadra ucraina è poi costretto a lasciare il campo tra le lacrime, poco dopo la mezz'ora, per un problema fisico. Un duro colpo per lo Shakhar anche se paradossalmente da quel momento arrivano le occasioni più nitide per gli ospiti. Al 40' rischio Inter con la parata in tuffo di Martinez sul colpo di testa di Bondar nato dagli sviluppi di un calcio d'angolo. Poi al 44' altra occasione da gol ma il tiro di Ocheretko è di poco a lato. Sicuramente un buon approccio per i nerazzurri che però non riescono a mantenere lo stesso ritmo per tutta la prima frazione di gioco. Così il primo tempo si chiude in parità, fermi su uno 0-0 che lascia aperta ogni possibilità. Anche ad inizio ripresa, l'Inter fatica a bucare le maglie della retroguardia. Così Chivu prova a cambiare l'inerzia della partita, toglie Calhanoglu, Spence e Dimarco per Zielinski, Diouf e Bisseck. L'Inter alza il ritmo, la squadra percepisce un po' di difficoltà dello Shakhtar, cambia proprio atteggiamento. Al 20' Thuram dalla distanza prova un tiro a giro che viene neutralizzato da Riznyk. Si alza anche un po' la tensione in campo e a farne le spese è Bastoni che in una manciata di minuti prende due ammonizioni, viene espulso, e lascia i compagni per gli ultimi venti minuti in inferiorità numerica. Il primo giallo arriva su segnalazione del quarto uomo, il secondo per aver spinto in area di rigore avversaria un giocatore dello Shakhtar mettendogli le mani al volto. L'arbitro non ha dubbi estrae il secondo cartellino giallo e poi quello rosso. E l'Inter è costretta a stringere i denti e in trance agonistica, grazie anche ai cambi di Chivu che inserisce Mkhitaryan per Bonny, trova il gol del vantaggio. Passaggio morbido e pennellato proprio di Mkhitaryan per Carlos Augusto che di destro porta avanti l'Inter nel tripudio di San Siro. Al 39' Mkhitaryan sfiora il raddoppio: prima non riesce ad impattare bene un ottimo assist di Thuram, poi ci riprova con un destro ma non inquadra la porta di un soffio. Negli ultimi minuti lo Shakhtar va vicinissimo al pari ed è Martinez a salvare il risultato, questa volta tutto va come deve andare e l'Inter torna a vincere.

items.title: Bastoni espulso per una manata contro lo Shakhtar: cosa è successo
items.summary: Doppia ammonizione per il difensore nerazzurro. Mano sul volto dell’avversario
items.content:
Alessandro Bastoni lascia i compagni in dieci. Al 68 ’ della partita di Champions League contro lo Shakhtar Donetsk , sullo 0-0, il difensore dell’Inter è stato espulso. Doppio giallo nel giro di un paio di minuti: il secondo per una manata in faccia a Ocheretko , che lo marcava in mezzo all’area. Bastoni, per sfilarsi dalla marcatura, lo ha spinto con entrambe le mani, prendendolo sul volto. Il centrocampista degli ucraini, non appena ha sentito il contatto, ha accentuato il fallo inducendo l’arbitro a estrarre il secondo cartellino giallo.

L’ultimo rosso di Bastoni era stato nella fatidica partita dell’Italia contro la Bosnia-Erzegovina . Il match che ha segnato la terza mancata qualificazione consecutiva ai Mondiali per gli azzurri. In quell’occasione il difensore era entrato in ritardo sull’avversario nel tentativo di recuperarlo. Sempre lo scorso anno, un mese prima della gara con la nazionale, un’altra espulsione lo ha visto protagonista ma dall’altra parte: in Inter-Juventus di campionato Bastoni, dopo una lieve trattenuta di Kalulu all’avambraccio, si era lasciato cadere spingendo l’arbitro a tirare fuori il secondo cartellino giallo contro il difensore bianconero. Dopo l’espulsione, il calciatore dell’Inter aveva esultato in modo plateale, suscitando molte critiche.

items.title: Huge crowds watch attempt to rescue shark stranded in South Korean canal
items.summary: It is thought the shark may have been drawn to the canal by unusually warm water and plenty of fish.
items.content:
Huge crowds have flocked to a canal in South Korea to watch a stranded shark.

The 9ft 10in (3m) shark, nicknamed Bukangi, was first spotted in the waterway last month in the south-eastern city of Busan.

Early on Thursday morning local time, South Korea's oceans ministry said the shark had been successfully guided out of the canal. By Friday however, it was still lingering at the canal's entrance, local media reported.

It is thought the shark may have been drawn to the canal by unusually warm water and plenty of fish.

The BBC's Seoul correspondent Jake Kwon goes to Busan to follow the latest attempt to rescue Bukangi, who has since been successfully guided out of the canal.

items.title: Ex-prosecutor charged with treason in Mexico over US drug raid
items.summary: César Jáuregui Moreno is accused of allowing US agents to join a raid on a suspected drugs lab in April.
items.content:
Federal prosecutors in Mexico have charged a former state prosecutor with treason for allowing US agents to join a raid on a suspected drugs lab in April without proper authorisation.

César Jáuregui Moreno served as attorney general of the northern border state of Chihuahua from 2023 to this year.

The involvement of Americans came to light after two US agents said to have worked for the CIA died in a car crash in Chihuahua along with two Mexican law enforcement officers.

Attorney General Ernestina Godoy Ramos said Jáuregui had allowed foreign agents to carry out activities reserved for Mexican authorities and had failed to share information. Jáuregui has denied the allegations.

The former prosecutor, who is a member of the conservative opposition PAN party, was arrested at the weekend. A court hearing is scheduled for Saturday.

A judge must still determine whether there is enough evidence to proceed with the case, Reuters news agency reports.

Jáuregui also faces state-level charges in Chihuahua, including of abuse of public office. In a court hearing for those charges on Sunday, he denied that he instructed or consented to the involvement of US agents in the operation.

Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum has come under pressure from US President Donald Trump to crack down on drug trafficking but has repeatedly declined offers of US-led counter-narcotics operations in the country.

She has been adamant that foreign officials can only operate on Mexican soil if given prior clearance by the federal government, and has insisted the Latin American nation's sovereignty should not be breached.

The crash occurred on 19 April, when a convoy returning from an operation targeting suspected methamphetamine labs in a remote, mountainous area veered off the road and plunged into a ravine.

Two members of the Chihuahua State Investigation Agency were killed along with the Americans, officials said.

At the time, in his capacity as state attorney general, Jáuregui told a news conference that the Americans had been "instructor officers" from the US embassy engaged in "training work as part of the general and normal exchange we have with the US authorities".

US media have reported that the two individuals worked for the CIA as part of an expanded effort to combat narcotics trafficking in the region.

Mexico says US agents killed in crash weren't permitted to operate there

items.title: Pope does not need further treatment after lung cancer surgery
items.summary: Test results have confirmed his diagnosis as a lung adenocarcinoma that was localised.
items.content:
Pope Leo XIV does not need any further treatment following an operation to remove a cancerous growth from his lung, his doctors have said.

Test results on tissue removed during surgery confirmed he had had a lung adenocarcinoma, as was initially diagnosed, and that the disease was localised, according to a statement shared by the Vatican.

"A subsequent oncological assessment has confirmed that no further treatment is necessary," it added.

The 71-year-old was discharged from Rome's Gemelli Hospital over the weekend four days after his operation - stopping to speak to well-wishers as he left the grounds.

It comes as he held his first weekly general audience since leaving hospital at St Peter's Square on Wednesday.

The surgery, which took place on 13 October and lasted for 90 minutes, included the removal of the lower lobe of the Pope's right lung.

The pontiff himself had announced during his weekly Sunday prayers that he would be having the procedure - telling those gathered in St Peter's Square that doctors had found a nodule on his lung.

He said at the time that it had been caught "at an early stage".

Images shared days after his operation, on Friday, showed the Pope celebrating Mass from the hospital wearing green vestments and standing behind a makeshift altar.

On the same day, the Vatican said he spoke to Russian President Vladimir Putin over the phone to urge a ceasefire in the blockaded Russian-occupied Ukrainian city of Oleshky to allow the delivery of food aid, and to call for "dialogue and peace".

The pontiff had a similar phone call with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky on Monday.

Those close to the Pope have also previously said he was keen not to delay a trip to Latin America which is planned for early November.

items.title: Rosenberg: US diplomatic push offers little hope for imminent Ukraine peace
items.summary: President Vladimir Putin does not feel under pressure right now to end the war, the BBC's Russia Editor writes.
items.content:
After two days of diplomacy – in Norway's capital and Russia's St Petersburg – is the war in Ukraine any closer to ending?

"Good and constructive" is how Norway's prime minister described Tuesday's talks between Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, US President Trump's special envoy Steve Witkoff and European representatives.

In Oslo, the idea of a trilateral meeting at leaders' level was floated. The hope was that Steve Witkoff's trip to Russia would pave the way for President Vladimir Putin, Zelensky and Trump to meet and agree an end to the fighting.

But Putin has shown little desire to share a table with Zelensky - unless that table is in Moscow.

The Kremlin says it may be willing to resume trilateral talks next month in Abu Dhabi, but only at the technical level.

In a post on X, Steve Witkoff himself conceded that "there is still important work to do", though he claimed "President Trump remains committed to seeing this war end..."

Russia says it is ready to resume talks with Ukraine and US to end war

US citizen Stephen Hubbard freed by Russia as Trump envoy meets Putin

For me, the most telling statement of the day was from Vladimir Putin's foreign policy aide Yuri Ushakov. He took part in the St Petersburg talks.

Ushakov said that Steve Witkoff had told President Putin about the discussions in Oslo and (as Witkoff viewed them) "new approaches from the Europeans and Kyiv".

The Kremlin adviser was clearly unimpressed by what he heard.

"In terms of resolving the Ukraine crisis, there wasn't much there that was useful," commented Ushakov.

Later Russian state TV asked him about the prospects for peace.

"I don't know how close we are getting," Yuri Ushakov said, "but things are moving in that direction."

It seems that President Putin doesn't feel under pressure right now to end the war.

He knows that Ukraine's air defences are under severe strain.

He knows that winter is coming and may well view the cold weather as an opportunity to pound Ukraine into submission.

He knows, too, that there is a US president in the White House who clearly wants a bigger, better, more profitable relationship with Moscow.

In recent days Donald Trump has paused some sanctions on Moscow, has agreed to buy Russian diesel and expressed biting criticism of President Zelensky.

That suits Russia just fine. It eases the pressure on the Kremlin leader.

"Right now Trump is the only leader in the Western world who is doing something for peace," Russian MP and TV anchor Evgeny Popov says.

"Doing something for peace, but a peace on your terms?" I respond. "Is that what you want?"

But in China next month a meeting between Vladimir Putin, Donald Trump and Xi Jinping may well take place on the fringes of the Apec summit.

Some commentators here are already dubbing it "The New Yalta" - a reference to the Yalta Conference of 1945, where Stalin, Churchill and Roosevelt met to plan the political and territorial reorganisation of post-war Europe.

"Russia, China and the United States are the only superpowers right now in the world," Evgeny Popov says. "Of course, it will be good for the entire world if our leaders meet in China."

After nearly five years of war, that would put Vladimir Putin exactly where he wants to be - at the top table of global politics.

items.title: I medici del Papa: 'Non ha bisogno di ulteriori terapie'
items.summary: Arrivato il referto dell'istologico. Leone in papamobile, ritorno alla normalità
items.content:
"Non è necessaria alcuna ulteriore terapia": s ono i medici del Papa a rassicurare che Leone sta bene , anche alla luce dell'atteso referto dell'esame istologico. La notizia è arrivata alla fine di una giornata che aveva segnato il ritorno di Leone alla normalità, con l'udienza generale a Piazza San Pietro, preceduta da un giro in papamobile, nonostante il maltempo su Roma.

I medici del Papa, il suo personal e, il dottor Luigi Carbone , e il chirurgo che lo ha operato al Policlinico Gemelli, il professor Stefano Margaritora , hanno comunicato che " sono stati refertati gli esami istologici definitivi e le indagini di biologia molecolare sul materiale asportato durante l'intervento chirurgico al Santo Padre . Gli esiti hanno confermato che si trattava di un adenocarcinoma polmonare e che la malattia era localizzata. Una successiva valutazione oncologica ha confermato che non è necessaria alcuna ulteriore terapia".

Una buona notizia che conferma quell'ottimismo che era trapelato già alla fine della degenza del Pontefice , con un ritorno a casa anticipato rispetto alle previsioni. Diventa più probabile ora anche quel desiderato viaggio in Sudamerica che il Papa dovrebbe effettuare a novembre, tra U ruguay, Argentin a e soprattutto il Perù dove Prevost ha vissuto vent'anni. Oggi il Papa è apparso sorridente e, a soli otto giorni dall'intervento al polmone, è voluto tornare in mezzo alla folla con il giro si saluti in papamobile. Unica precauzione il tettuccio trasparente sulla vettura bianca per proteggerlo dall'acqua. L'unico riferimento al problema attraversato è nelle prime parole che pronuncia in piazza: "La prima cosa che vorrei dirvi è grazie! Grazie per il sostegno delle vostre preghiere. Grazie a Dio per la sua generosità. Rinnoviamo tutti la nostra fiducia nella bontà, nella misericordia di Di o", dice ai 30 mila fedeli presenti per la catechesi settimanale del Papa.

Prima dell'udienza generale aveva anche incontrato, nella Sala Clementina , i partecipanti ad un convegno sui nuovi santi, segnando così un ritorno alle attività quotidiane, quasi come prima dell'intervento. Quasi, perché comunque gli incontri restano parcellizzati e, al momento, più corti rispetto al normale. E ' quella "graduale" ripresa che aveva annunciato lo stesso Leone all'Angelus di domenica, il giorno dopo avere lasciato il Gemelli. Dal viso traspare qualche segno di stanchezza, quasi impercettibile, ma il Papa non rinuncia a nulla: alla fine dell'udienza generale guida anche il canto del 'Padre Nostro' e come sempre saluta individualmente le persone ammesse al cosiddetto 'baciamano'.

items.title: Nigeria's first Ebola patient holidayed in Uganda, officials say
items.summary: The wife of a diplomat based in Abuja travelled to Kampala for a vacation.
items.content:
Nigeria's first confirmed case of Ebola since the outbreak in East Africa began in May is the wife of a diplomat who travelled to Uganda's capital for a holiday, the head of Africa's health agency has told the BBC.

The woman is originally from Uganda but based in Abuja, where she fell ill three days after arriving home in the Nigerian capital on 3 October, according to Dr Jean Kaseya from the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention.

Nigeria's health minister has confirmed to the BBC the 42-year-old patient spent two and a half weeks in Kampala, adding that she also made a two-hour stopover in Ethiopia's capital on her return.

The authorities were working to prevent the virus from spreading and had identified 44 people who had been in contact with the woman, who tested positive for Ebola on Tuesday, the minister said.

"Not all of them have been in close proximity. We cast the net wide so that we contain it as broadly as possible," Pate told the BBC.

What is Ebola and why is stopping the latest outbreak so difficult?

None of the contacts, who are now in isolation, are known to have developed symptoms, including the person the patient travelled with, the health minister said, adding that the woman had not travelled outside Abuja since landing.

Kaseya explained that the woman had first developed symptoms on 6 October when she had sought medical help.

"She went to the first hospital, a private hospital, thinking that she had malaria, and then she went to the second private hospital. She was admitted on the 11th," he told the BBC's Newshour programme.

Malaria is endemic in Nigeria and its symptoms - a high temperature, headaches, muscle aches, vomiting and or diarrhoea - are similar to those of Ebola.

After her condition failed to improve, public health authorities were alerted on Monday 19 October, Pate said.

Her diagnosis was confirmed the next day following three laboratory tests, he said.

The incubation period for Ebola ranges from two to 21 days, meaning those exposed to the virus may not become ill for several weeks.

Ebola is a rare but deadly disease , external caused by a virus. As the disease progresses, vomiting and diarrhoea develop and it can lead to organ failure. Some, but not all, patients develop internal and external bleeding.

The disease spreads from one person to another by contact with infected bodily fluids such as blood or vomit.

The outbreak in Democratic Republic of Congo, which began in May, has claimed at least 4,600 lives, with more than 9,500 cases recorded, the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control reports , external .

Shortly after the outbreak was announced, it was also reported in Uganda, where at least two people died. Uganda declared itself free of the disease in August after its last patient was discharged.

There have been conflicting accounts about the patient in Nigeria and her movements.

Pate and Kaseya's comments contradict a statement issued earlier by the Ugandan ministry of health, which described the woman as a Nigerian national who had gone to eastern DR Congo for business, only transiting through Uganda.

It insisted there were currently no confirmed active Ebola cases in the country and that the woman's passage through Uganda did not mean she had contracted the virus there.

Nigeria's health minister and the Africa CDC chief have sought to play down any tension.

Pate said Nigerian officials were working with Uganda, Ethiopia and the Africa CDC to establish the full facts.

"We respect our sister nation of Uganda," he said. "We have very strong solidarity, we are all in it together."

Kaseya also urged African countries to share information, saying this would help investigators trace the woman's movements and establish where she might have contracted the virus.

And he encouraged Western countries not to impose travel restrictions, saying "collaboration and solidarity" were the way to help stop the current outbreak.

The disease recently spread to Kenya, which has reported at least nine infections.

On Monday, the US advised its citizens to reconsider travel to Kenya because of health risks and raised its travel advisory level for the country.

In 2014, Nigeria successfully contained an Ebola outbreak , which had resulted in 20 confirmed cases and eight deaths.

Pate expressed confidence in the country's ability to repeat that success, citing strengthened disease surveillance, laboratories and thousands of trained epidemiologists.

"Nigeria has muscle memory that has been activated, but we are not fighting the past outbreak in the exactly the same way. We have to be vigilant," he said.

The outbreak in DR Congo has been caused by the Bundibugyo species of Ebola, which is relatively rare, with no approved vaccine or treatment - though trials are under way.

items.title: Rust Style Guide
items.summary: Article URL: https://google.github.io/styleguide/rustguide.html Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50186010 Points: 266 # Comments: 146
items.content:
This document is a style guide for the usage of the Rust programming language at Google. In this context, “style” refers to more than just formatting; it includes guidance on API and implementation design.

Rust is used in many places, including google3 , Android, ChromeOS, Fuchsia, and Chrome, and we’d like for Rust usage at Google to be consistent both within and across codebases. In addition to bringing consistency to our Rust code, style guidance also helps establish a standard of quality.

The current scope of authority of the rules outlined in this guide:

By and large, we have this document for the same reasons we have a C++ style guide .

Most style rules come from one or more of the goals listed below.

We expect our code to be around for long periods of time, and we consider a little bit of extra effort applied during code writing to be worth it in the long run if the style rule improves readability.

Large-Scale Changes (LSCs) are common at Google, and consistency helps make LSCs easier to carry out.

The broader Rust ecosystem already has a pretty good amount of consistency in style, and we should rely on that where possible to reduce surprise and make it less work to learn Google’s Rust style.

Every Rust developer and reviewer at Google has to keep these style rules in mind: as such, we should be careful to include rules that have a tangible benefit.

There are many cases where reasonable people may disagree about a style, and we expect that disagreement to show up often on CLs. Having a style rule helps avoid having to rehash this each time. Rules in this category that do not have other benefits should be kept to a minimum.

Follow the official public Rust style rules to the extent they don’t conflict with this style guide.

A “conflict” would be a case where this style guide suggests a pattern that is discouraged, or counter to the primary encouraged pattern in the Rust style guide.

Why does the guidance in this style guide deviate from regular Rust style rules?

Most style guides have three goals: consistency, readability, and encouraging good API design. Regardless of the specific choices made, it helps everyone to have these choices made beforehand to limit bikeshedding.

This style guide shares those goals, but it also has an additional goal not seen as often: smoothing the way for Large-Scale Changes (LSCs). Large codebases like many of the ones at Google occasionally need to run codebase-spanning refactorings that are assisted by tooling: for this to work well, the code should be something tooling has an easy time working with. Consistency helps for this, but so does having deliberate refactor-friendly patterns.

When applying rules that relate to API design, you should distinguish two types of code:

For library code , style guide rules that concern API design are binding.

For application code , the rules on API design are a strong recommendation. As you apply them, keep in mind that since application code is written to solve a specific problem, it should generally favor simplicity and directness over broad reusability. Avoid premature generalization and abstraction; focus on what is required to meet the immediate need.

A crate is a unit of compilation. A crate always contains a nameless Rust module, the “root module”.

A Rust module is a unit of code organization within a crate. Rust modules are used to control visibility of names. Modules can be nested. They can also be used to split code across files and directories.

The following sections convey that in Chromium, it is preferable to not make use of all possibilities of splitting modules across files.

Prefer small crates in Chromium; ideally, but not necessarily, a single file (focusing on one abstraction). If your code can be split up into small crates, do so.

A crate corresponds to a single rust_static_library (chrome) rule, which may contain one or more .rs files.

The root module is allowed to re-export public APIs from leaf submodules , making submodules an implementation detail of the crate (as users don’t need to know about these submodules).

This rule about small crates applies equally to crates with and without submodules. First, evaluate whether the APIs need to be in the same crate, and only then consider whether submodules could help organize the APIs.

If you decide to use submodules, follow the expected file structure .

Larger crates are allowed when trait impl coherence rules force multiple types and traits to be included in one library, or if you’re building a large foundational library.

Fine-grained library targets are recommended in Chromium due to the massive size of our codebase, non-local effects of adding dependencies in the build graph, and to improve performance of parallel compilation and build caching.

In Chromium .rs source files belonging to one rust_library (one Rust crate) must reside in a single directory.

Don’t use subdirectories to organize files that belong to a single crate. If organizing one crate’s files into subdirectories feels necessary, this is a strong indication that the crate has grown too large and should be split.

This crate layout is intentionally different from the conventional Cargo directory structure typically used in open-source repositories.

Exception: Rust code in //third_party that is also built with Cargo should follow the conventional Cargo directory structure.

The approach in Chromium is driven by the following factors:

When a leaf module has a primary user-defined item (e.g., Foo ), the module should be named after that item (e.g., mod foo and foo.rs ).

Leaf modules that are not primarily about any particular abstraction can be named as desired.

This makes it easy to identify the content/purpose of a source file or leaf module at a glance.

The only items in non-leaf modules should be module declarations (not definitions) and re-exports .

Note that the definition of leaf modules allows the following sub-modules: mod test and cross-language binding modules like #[cxx::bridge] .

This makes it easier to find things, and avoids mixing structure and contents.

Don’t use glob imports, except in the following situations where you may optionally do so at your own discretion:

C++ interop: Since the same namespace (in C++) is a submodule in different Rust crates (in Rust), you may merge the namespaces into a private copy using glob imports. For example:

In this hypothetical example, you can use absl::Status and absl::StrCat from Rust, the same way you would from C++, instead of spelling them as status::absl::Status and strings::absl::StrCat .

This must only be used for merging C++ namespaces, and the resulting merged module must not be public.

If using third-party crates that encourage a prelude, it is up to the reviewer’s discretion to allow it.

Glob imports increase toil for code janitors running LSCs, and make it harder to know where a type comes from in contexts without xrefs.

This rule corresponds to the rustfmt setting imports_granularity = Module .

Basically, there should not be any :: ’s inside the {..} block of a use statement. For example:

Import traits within function bodies, unless the trait’s methods are used extensively throughout the file.

To use top-level functions defined in other modules or crates, import their module and call them with modulename::functionname() . For example:

In Chromium, when importing functions from small, single-purpose first-party crates .

Many Rust codebases consistently keep a style such that unqualified lowercase names are assumed local, so foo() can be assumed to be from the same module. This rule largely exists to avoid reviewer disagreements, the benefit is mostly consistency and a minor edge on reading code without xrefs.

By default, types and traits should be referenced in code without using their module path, e.g., code should use Regex , not regex::Regex , with a use regex::Regex at the top of the file or potentially in the relevant function.

Use the appropriate formatting tool (e.g., git cl format in Chromium).

A codebase may choose to not apply the following rustfmt options if they care about building on stable and the option is unavailable on their stable Rust:

Usage of lowercase alphabets in hex literals ( 0xab123cdef as opposed to 0xAB123CDEF ): hex_literal_case = Lower

Usage of escapes for invisible characters in literals. E.g., if you wish to have text containing a Zero-Width joiner, use \u{200D} .

You may opt out of automatic formatting using #[rustfmt::skip] , but only in the following situations:

Important: Formatting should not be skipped for personal style choices.

Prefer unique ownership and borrowing over Rc and Arc for managing memory.

Generally, Rust allows representing object graphs without using shared ownership smart pointers. These pointers add runtime overhead and their own unique complexity. Engineers coming from other languages might tend to use Rc and Arc too quickly.

Use .clone() when you genuinely need a deep copy of an object.

Avoid using .clone() as a substitute for borrowing. Design code that works naturally with Rust’s ownership and borrowing rules. However, if the borrowing relationships become excessively complex, .clone() can be a pragmatic choice.
